Roll back the producer schema change immediately — revert to emitting events without session_id. Then follow a breaking change protocol: publish the proposed schema to a schema registry with FULL compatibility enforcement, get consumer sign-off from all 8 teams, then coordinate a migration window.

The 3 failing consumers are at fault for not handling missing fields defensively — all JSON consumers should use .get() instead of direct key access. The platform team should document the new field and allow consumers to update on their own schedule.
Coordinate an emergency simultaneous deployment: deploy the 3 failing consumers with session_id support at the same moment as the producer, eliminating the window where the field is missing.
explanation: Option B is the correct response: roll back the breaking change first, then follow the proper protocol. A rollback is the fastest path to stopping ongoing consumer failures and is the standard incident response for an uncoordinated breaking schema change. After stabilization, the correct path is schema registry enforcement with FULL compatibility — the platform team cannot deploy a breaking schema change without the registry blocking it and consumer sign-off being recorded. Option A (hot-patch) stops the bleeding for 3 consumers but accepts the broken state and leaves the structural cause unaddressed; it also does not fix the 5 consumers who may access session_id in future code changes. Option C incorrectly assigns fault to consumers: when a producer makes an uncoordinated breaking change, the producer is at fault — consumers are entitled to rely on the documented schema contract, and defensive coding is good practice but does not excuse a unilateral breaking change. Option D (simultaneous emergency deploy) is operationally risky: coordinating deployment across 8 consumer teams simultaneously is difficult, and any timing gap (even seconds) exposes consumers to the missing required field.
hints: Three consumers are failing in production right now. What is the fastest action to stop the ongoing failures before addressing the structural root cause?
Which structural change makes it technically impossible for the platform team to deploy a required-field addition without all consumers being verified as compatible first?

title: CDC Pipeline Produces 3.7% Duplicate Rows After Rolling Deploy — Offset Reset to Earliest
scenario_context: A Kafka CDC pipeline consumes from a topic with 5 partitions. Consumer offsets are committed synchronously after each message is processed and written to the warehouse. A rolling deploy restarts consumer pods one by one. After the deploy, the warehouse shows 3.7% duplicate rows in the last 2 hours. Investigation reveals the consumer group's committed offsets for partitions 2 and 4 reset to the earliest available offset during the deploy.
description: What is the most likely root cause of the offset reset and how is it prevented?
options: The root cause is synchronous offset commits being too slow: pods restart faster than offsets can be committed. In-flight messages with uncommitted offsets are re-delivered after restart. Fix: switch to asynchronous offset commits to reduce the commit latency window.

The root cause is auto.offset.reset=earliest: when the consumer group has no committed offset record for partitions 2 and 4 (e.g., those pods had not yet committed any offsets in the current session before they were restarted), Kafka falls back to earliest and replays the full partition history. Fix: set auto.offset.reset=latest and ensure all partitions commit initial offsets before a rolling deploy.

The root cause is the rolling deploy triggering rebalances: when pods restart, Kafka reassigns partitions to surviving pods. The reassigned pods start from a stale committed offset because the commit cycle was interrupted by the rebalance. Fix: use static group membership (group.instance.id) to prevent unnecessary rebalances.

The root cause is writing to the warehouse before committing the offset: a pod killed after writing but before committing causes re-delivery and a duplicate write. Fix: commit the offset before writing (pre-commit) to prevent re-delivery.
explanation: Option B most precisely explains the observed pattern — a reset to earliest for specific partitions (2 and 4 only, not all 5). This is characteristic of auto.offset.reset=earliest triggered when the consumer group has no committed offset record for those partitions. During a rolling deploy, if the pods owning partitions 2 and 4 are restarted before they ever committed an offset in the current session (e.g., they had just received those partitions from a recent rebalance and processed messages but not yet committed), Kafka finds no committed offset for those partitions and falls back to earliest — replaying the full partition history. The fix is setting auto.offset.reset=latest (for partitions with no committed offset, start at the current end rather than the beginning) and ensuring initial offsets are committed promptly after partition assignment. Option A (synchronous commits too slow) would cause re-delivery of recently processed messages, not a full reset to the earliest offset. Option C (static group membership) reduces rebalance frequency but does not address the auto.offset.reset behavior when offsets are absent. Option D (pre-commit) would introduce message loss (not duplicates) — it is the wrong trade-off direction.
hints: Partitions 2 and 4 reset to the earliest offset — the beginning of the partition history, not just the most recent uncommitted messages. What Kafka setting causes this specific behavior when no committed offset is found for a partition?
When would a consumer group have no committed offset record for specific partitions during a rolling deploy?

title: Append-Only vs. Upsert for a Financial Fact Table That Receives Correction Events
scenario_context: A financial pipeline receives two event types from the source system: (1) original transaction events and (2) correction events that update the amount on a prior transaction (approximately 0.5% of transactions receive a correction within 72 hours). The team must decide how the warehouse handles corrections: (A) append-only — insert both the original and correction events; aggregate with correction semantics at query time; (B) upsert — apply the correction as an UPDATE to the original row in the fact table, keeping only the latest amount.
description: Which approach is more defensible for a financial fact table, and why?
options: Upsert is more defensible: maintaining the latest correct amount in a single fact row simplifies BI queries — consumers need no knowledge of correction event semantics. The 0.5% correction rate is low enough that upsert overhead is negligible.

Append-only is more defensible: preserving both the original and the correction event provides a complete audit trail of every state change. Corrections are reconciled via window functions or event_type aggregation at query time. The design is immutable and requires no row-level updates.
The choice depends on the warehouse technology: upsert via MERGE is cost-efficient in Snowflake or BigQuery; append-only is the natural choice for an object store like S3 with Iceberg or Delta Lake.

Neither is appropriate for financial corrections: corrections should be written to a dedicated corrections table and joined to the fact table at reporting time, keeping the original fact table unmodified and the correction logic fully explicit.
explanation: Option B is more defensible for a financial fact table governed by audit requirements. Append-only preserves every event that occurred — the original transaction and the correction — giving auditors a complete timeline of what amounts were recorded, when, and when corrections were applied. This is the event sourcing principle applied to financial data: facts are immutable; corrections are new facts, not overwrites. Upsert (Option A) permanently destroys the original event's amount — after an UPDATE, auditors cannot determine what the original amount was or when the correction was applied. For financial data subject to regulatory audit, this loss of historical state is a compliance risk. Option C (technology-dependent) frames the choice around operational convenience rather than governance requirements — the correct design for auditable financial data is append-only regardless of technology, and both Snowflake and Iceberg support append-only semantics. Option D (separate corrections table) is a valid variant of the append-only pattern used in some financial systems, but it adds join complexity without improving upon Option B's correctness or auditability properties.
hints: If a correction is applied as an UPDATE to the original fact row, what information is permanently lost from the warehouse?
A financial auditor needs to reconstruct exactly what was recorded at each point in time, including the original amount before any corrections. Which design supports this?

title: Multi-Region Synchronous Replication Causes SLA Breach — Switching to Async
scenario_context: A platform team replicates a Postgres database (500 GB, 1,000 writes/second) from US-East-1 to EU-West-1 for GDPR data residency compliance using synchronous replication: every write is confirmed only after the EU replica acknowledges. Cross-region round-trip latency is 90ms, adding 90ms to every write. The write-path p95 latency SLA is 50ms. The SLA is breached. The team proposes switching to asynchronous replication.
description: What is the correct trade-off analysis, and which design should the team choose?
options: Switch to asynchronous replication: it removes the 90ms cross-region round-trip from the write path, resolving the SLA breach. The explicit trade-off is a potential data loss window — if the primary fails after a write is acknowledged locally but before the EU replica receives it, those writes are lost.

Keep synchronous replication and provision a higher-throughput database instance in both regions: faster hardware reduces the replication round-trip below 50ms, meeting the SLA without introducing any data loss risk.
Add a CDN layer in front of the write path: CDN edge nodes accept writes locally and replicate asynchronously to both regions, achieving sub-50ms write latency with synchronous durability semantics.

Replace synchronous replication with a Kafka-based CDC pipeline: CDC is inherently asynchronous, removes the 90ms write-path penalty, and provides at-least-once delivery guarantees that effectively match synchronous replication durability for financial data.
explanation: Option A correctly identifies the trade-off and the correct design: asynchronous replication removes the cross-region round-trip from the write path, restoring p95 latency below 50ms. The explicit cost is a potential data loss window of up to 90ms + processing time if the primary fails after acknowledging a write but before the EU replica receives it. This is the canonical synchronous-vs-asynchronous distributed systems trade-off, and the team must explicitly accept the data loss risk given the SLA requirement. Option B (faster hardware) is not possible: the 90ms cross-region round-trip is determined by the speed of light between US-East-1 and EU-West-1, not by database hardware. No hardware upgrade reduces a physical network latency constant. Option C (CDN for writes) is incorrect: CDNs are designed for read caching, not write durability. A write 'accepted' at a CDN edge with async replication to both regions provides neither synchronous durability nor strong consistency. Option D (Kafka CDC) removes write-path latency but does not provide synchronous durability: at-least-once delivery can still produce duplicate events, and Kafka CDC introduces additional complexity and a replication lag — it is not equivalent to synchronous replication.
hints: The 90ms latency is the speed of light across the Atlantic — no hardware upgrade can reduce it. What is the only architectural change that removes this fixed network cost from the write path?
If the team accepts asynchronous replication, what is the worst-case data loss scenario if the primary region fails at exactly the wrong moment?

title: Airflow vs. Event-Driven Triggers for 500+ DAGs at Scale — When Does Migrating Make Sense?
description: A data platform team operates 500 Airflow DAGs. The Airflow scheduler is at 80% CPU and occasionally misses 1-minute schedule intervals. The team evaluates two options: (A) scale the Airflow scheduler — larger instance, more workers; (B) migrate high-volume DAGs to event-driven triggers — Kafka events trigger DAG runs instead of cron. A senior engineer argues event-driven is always better at scale. Which response is most accurate?
options: The senior engineer is correct: Airflow's cron-based scheduler does not scale past a few hundred DAGs without degrading. Event-driven triggers are always superior for data pipelines at 500+ DAGs.

Airflow scheduling scales horizontally with additional schedulers — adding scheduler instances resolves the CPU bottleneck without any architectural change. Event-driven triggers are only necessary when pipelines must react to real-time events with sub-second latency.

The correct choice is DAG-type-dependent: DAGs that are data-triggered (start when upstream data is ready) benefit from event-driven patterns because they can start immediately when data arrives rather than polling on a cron interval. DAGs that are genuinely time-based (run at 3 AM regardless of data state) gain no benefit from event-driven patterns. Migrating all 500 DAGs indiscriminately adds operational complexity without benefit for the time-based subset.

At 500 DAGs, the root cause of scheduler CPU overload is DAG proliferation. The correct fix is consolidating multiple DAGs into fewer, larger DAGs — consolidation always resolves scheduler overhead better than architectural changes.
explanation: Option C is the most nuanced and defensible answer. The scheduler CPU issue is real and needs addressing, but the correct solution depends on DAG type. Data-triggered DAGs (e.g., 'run when the transactions table is ready') benefit directly from event-driven patterns: they start immediately when upstream data signals readiness, reducing latency and eliminating wasted polls on a cron interval when data is not yet ready. Time-based DAGs (e.g., 'run at 3 AM daily regardless of data state') do not benefit from event-driven patterns — the trigger event for '3 AM daily' is the clock, which Airflow's scheduler already handles. Migrating time-based DAGs to Kafka-triggered runs adds topic management complexity with zero benefit. Option A overstates Airflow's scaling limitations: Airflow 2.x with a distributed scheduler and proper resource allocation supports hundreds to low thousands of DAGs. Option B overstates horizontal scaling — adding schedulers addresses the CPU symptom but not the root cause if many DAGs could be event-driven. Option D (consolidation) may be appropriate in specific cases but is not universally the correct fix — many workloads have legitimate reasons for separate DAGs.
hints: Some of the 500 DAGs trigger when upstream data is ready; others trigger at a fixed time regardless of data state. Does the event-driven pattern benefit both types equally?
For a DAG scheduled to run at 3 AM daily regardless of data state, what benefit does replacing the Airflow cron trigger with a Kafka event trigger provide?

title: Data Lineage Tracing vs. Lineage Propagation — Different Capabilities or the Same?
description: A data governance team is deploying a lineage system. The lead distinguishes two modes: (A) lineage tracing — given an output artifact (a dashboard metric or a warehouse column), traverse the lineage graph backwards to identify every source that contributed to it; (B) lineage propagation — when a source dataset changes (schema change, data quality alert, deletion), traverse forward and actively notify all downstream artifacts that depend on it. A junior engineer argues these are the same capability traversed in opposite directions. Which response is most accurate?
options: They are the same capability in opposite directions: a lineage graph can be traversed backwards (tracing) or forwards (propagation). Any system that supports one direction implicitly supports the other with no additional implementation.

They are distinct operational modes: lineage tracing is a read-only, on-demand graph traversal; lineage propagation is an event-driven notification system that must be triggered by source change events and must deliver notifications to all registered downstream consumers. A lineage graph alone is insufficient for propagation — it also requires an event bus and a subscriber registry.

Lineage tracing is the governance use case (auditing, root-cause analysis); lineage propagation is a data catalog feature for impact analysis. They are separate products and should not be conflated in a single lineage system.

Lineage propagation is a superset of lineage tracing: any system capable of propagating changes forward must have a complete lineage graph, so implementing propagation automatically provides tracing as well.
explanation: Option B is correct: the two modes are distinct in operational requirements beyond graph traversal direction. Lineage tracing is a read-only query against a lineage graph — given an artifact, find its ancestors. This is point-in-time, on-demand, and passive: the graph is queried when a user or system requests it. Lineage propagation is active: it must detect that a source has changed (event detection), traverse the graph forward to find all downstream consumers, and deliver notifications or trigger actions (event bus, subscriber registry, delivery guarantees). A static lineage graph supports tracing but requires additional infrastructure — event bus, subscriber management, delivery confirmation — for propagation. Option A is incorrect: graph traversal direction is technically reversible, but the operational requirements for active notification delivery are fundamentally different from read-only graph traversal. Option C incorrectly partitions these as separate products — propagation depends on the same lineage graph used for tracing; they are complementary features of one system, not separate products. Option D is incorrect: propagation requires a complete lineage graph, but having a complete graph does not automatically provide a queryable tracing interface — the delivery and query systems are separate implementations.
hints: Lineage tracing is triggered by a user asking 'where did this metric come from?' Lineage propagation is triggered by a source change event. Do these two operations require the same technical components?
What does lineage propagation require that a lineage tracing query does not — something that must run actively and continuously when source changes occur?
